chapter.name: Life Processes in Plants
chapter.blurb: Plant growth, photosynthesis, transport of water and food, and respiration in plants.

concepts.name: How plants grow: sunlight and water
concepts.description: Changes seen as plants grow, and the experiment with three pots showing that sunlight and water are needed.
concepts.idea: Plants need both sunlight and water for their growth.
concepts.rule: As a plant grows, new leaves and branches emerge, its height increases and its stem thickens. In Activity 10.1 three pots with similar saplings are used: pot A in sunlight with water, pot B in sunlight without water, and pot C in the dark with water, observed for two weeks. Pot A grows best; the plant in C, which gets water but no sunlight, grows less; the plant in B, with sunlight but no water, may die. So plants require both sunlight and water for growth. Only one condition is changed between pots so that the effect of each factor can be judged. The ancient Indian text Vrikshayurveda records observations on plant growth, soil and farming, including methods of organic manure preparation.
concepts.example: The experiment takes two weeks and can be done with chilli or tomato saplings.

concepts.name: Leaves, chlorophyll and starch
concepts.description: Leaves as food factories, chlorophyll, the iodine test on a leaf and the role of light.
concepts.idea: Green leaves make starch in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll.
concepts.rule: Plants store food as starch, a carbohydrate, and it is made in leaves, which are generally broad and flat. Leaves are mostly green because of the pigment chlorophyll, which helps capture sunlight efficiently. In Activity 10.2 a leaf is boiled in water, placed in alcohol in a test tube in a beaker of boiling water until it is colourless, and then diluted iodine is dropped on it; blue-black shows starch. Alcohol must never be heated directly since it is flammable. Decolourising makes the colour change easy to see. In Activity 10.3, leaves with green and non-green patches from a plant kept in sunlight and one kept in the dark for 36 hours were tested; only the green patches of the leaf from sunlight turned blue-black, showing that chlorophyll and sunlight are needed to make starch. Leaves are called the food factories of plants. Some leaves look red, violet or brown because of other pigments that hide the green, and some of these also help photosynthesis.
concepts.example: A red-leaved plant can still test positive for starch.

concepts.name: Carbon dioxide and oxygen in photosynthesis
concepts.description: Testing the role of carbon dioxide with caustic soda, and the release of oxygen by a water plant.
concepts.idea: Plants need carbon dioxide from the air for food making and release oxygen.
concepts.rule: In Activity 10.4 a destarched leaf is half inserted into a bottle with caustic soda (sodium hydroxide), which absorbs carbon dioxide, and left in sunlight. The part outside turns blue-black with iodine, while the part inside does not, showing carbon dioxide from the air is essential for making starch. Caustic soda burns skin so only teachers handle it. Sunlight, water, chlorophyll and carbon dioxide are essential for food synthesis; the process in which plants prepare food in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll is called photosynthesis. A leaf is the primary site, but other green parts also photosynthesise. In Activity 10.5 a water plant under a funnel and inverted test tube in sunlight gives bubbles; a lit matchstick burns intensely in the gas, showing it is rich in oxygen. So oxygen is released during photosynthesis, which needs sunlight because the set-up in the dark does not produce bubbles.
concepts.example: Barkha didi's test with a matchstick showed oxygen.

concepts.name: Photosynthesis in a nutshell and stomata
concepts.description: The word equation of photosynthesis, glucose and storage as starch, stomata, and R. H. Dastur.
concepts.idea: Carbon dioxide + water, in sunlight and chlorophyll, give glucose + oxygen.
concepts.rule: Water, sunlight, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll are needed for photosynthesis, which produces glucose, a simple carbohydrate. Glucose is an instant source of energy and later gets converted into starch for storage. The word equation is: Carbon dioxide + Water, in sunlight with chlorophyll, gives Glucose + Oxygen. Water and minerals are taken by roots. Gas exchange takes place through tiny pores called stomata on the surface of the leaves; in Activity 10.6 a peel from the lower surface of a leaf is stained with ink and seen under a microscope. Stomata help in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during photosynthesis and respiration. Rustom Hormusji Dastur (1896-1961), head of the Botany Department at the Royal Institute of Science, Bombay, studied effects of water, temperature and the colour of light on photosynthesis.
concepts.example: Glucose made by plants is later stored as starch.

concepts.name: Transport of water and food in plants
concepts.description: The xylem carries water and minerals; the phloem carries food; the red ink experiment.
concepts.idea: Xylem carries water and minerals upward, and phloem carries food to all parts of the plant.
concepts.rule: Roots take up water and minerals from the soil. In Activity 10.7 a twig of a plant with white flowers is placed in red ink water and another in plain water. After a day, red colour appears in the stem, leaves and flowers of the twig in ink, and in the cut stem a red colour is seen in thin tube-like structures called the xylem. Minerals dissolved in water also travel up through the xylem, which is present in the stem, branches and leaves. The food made in leaves is carried to all parts through another set of thin tubes called the phloem, and may be stored in parts such as seeds and roots. Thus xylem transports water and minerals from roots to other parts, while phloem transports food from leaves.
concepts.example: White flowers turn red in the ink experiment.

concepts.name: Respiration in plants
concepts.description: Plants respire in all parts, the germinating seed and lime water activity, and comparison with photosynthesis.
concepts.idea: Plants break down glucose with oxygen to release energy, releasing carbon dioxide.
concepts.rule: In Activity 10.8 soaked moong seeds are kept on wet cotton in a flask in the dark for 24 hours and the flask is connected to lime water. The lime water turns milky, showing more carbon dioxide, which is produced by the seeds as they respire. During respiration glucose is broken down with oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and energy: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. The energy is used by plants for growth and development. All parts of a plant, green or non-green, respire. Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and gives glucose and oxygen, occurring in green parts in sunlight, while respiration uses glucose and oxygen and gives carbon dioxide, water and energy in all living parts. Photosynthesis and respiration keep a balance in nature. Kamala Sohonie (1911-1998) did remarkable work on respiration in plants and worked on the coconut palm sap drink Neera.
concepts.example: A sealed bottle garden shows the balance of the two processes.
